There's a particular pleasure in being asked to write anything at all—the blank page suddenly not an obligation but a door standing open. And yet the first instinct is to look for the "right" subject, as if topics were keys hidden under doormats. But there are no right subjects. There's only attention.

Take, for instance, the headlights that sweep across your bedroom wall late at night. You've never once thought about them as worth describing, and yet: they arrive at the edge of the ceiling, bend slowly down one wall like a hand feeling its way, linger, then slide away. Each car writes the same sentence and deletes it before you can read it. The room becomes briefly a planetarium, then goes dark again.

Everything is like this if you lean in. The sound a refrigerator makes when it decides to start working. The way a word you've typed a thousand times suddenly looks misspelled—"balance," say, which seems wrong no matter how many times you check it. The specific silence after a phone call ends, thicker than ordinary silence, still shaped like the conversation.

And this, maybe, is the whole secret of writing, if there is one: not finding remarkable things but refusing to look away from unremarkable ones until they admit to being strange. The world is not hiding its best material. It hands it out constantly, for free, in streetlight shadows and kettle steam, waiting for someone to pick it up and say, look at this.
